newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Crown's fall unlikely to harm banks-CNB official.
newsitem.headline: Crown's fall unlikely to harm banks-CNB official.

text.p: The recent sharp fall in the Czech crown is unlikely to harm the nations' banking system considerably, a senior central bank official said, even as analysts predicted lower profits and a rise in bankruptcies.

"We tried to calm down the situation so I do not expect any considerable detrimental effect on our banking system," Miroslav Hrncir, a member of the Czech National Bank's board, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
Hrncir was in Basle to attend the annual meeting of the Bank for International Settlements.

The Czech central bank in late May resorted to massive currency market intervention, dramatic interest rate hikes and restraints on foreigners' money market access to battle a speculative assault on the currency. In the end it freed the crown from its plus/minus 7.5 percent mark/dollar fixing basket.
While Hrncir explained the changeover to a more flexible foreign exchange regime was overdue, he noted the central bank took its steps under pressure.

"We maintained a nominal exchange rate that was unchanged from the very beginning of transition, so after six, seven years it was certainly time to adjust to a more flexible regime... but I must acknowledge we acted under some pressure," Hrncir said.
He added this left the currency open to speculative attacks which "could have some impact on our banking system."

Banking analysts said the crown's devaluation could lead to considerable losses on commercial banks' foreign exchange exposure, adding banks also faced the risk of non-payment of expensive floating rate loans.
But as the central bank acted quickly to limit the damage, the attack's impact should be marginal, Hrncir predicted.
"The policy of the central bank was to dimish the effect of the speculation, we tried to calm down the situation, so I do not expect any considerable detrimental effects on our banking system."

Since the turbulence erupted, central bank officials have been quick to play down its impact, denying the troubles confirmed errors in the Czech process of economic transformation or that the devaluation would hurt economic growth.
In fact, Czech Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said the new exchange rate could have benefits, as it is a way to improve conditions for the Czech trade balance.
While Hrncir and other policy makers said the lower crown rate may lead to slightly higher inflation rates, this effect should also not be overly dramatic.
Hrncir was confident inflation levels could be kept at single-digit levels this year, after a rate of around eight percent last year.
Speaking about efforts to privatise the nation's four largest banks, Hrncir said the process should be completed fairly soon and would not be compromised by recent events.
While the process would proceed in a case by case fashion, Hrncir said it "should move quite quickly," predicting "two of the four should be privatised in the course of one year."

He said the nation's former foreign trade bank Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka (CSOB) should be the first to be privatised while Czeska Sporitelna would likely be the last. Komercni Banka and Investicnic a Postovni Banka (IPB) are also undergoing privatisation.
